A five-minute illustrated talk
Prediction

Journey of a prompt

Google
Google suggests searches. An LLM predicts a token.
01 / TEXT

Split the prompt

A tokenizer breaks text into pieces it recognizes.

The · capital · of · France · is
02 / ADDRESS

Find each ID

Each piece has a fixed address in this vocabulary.

“ France” → ID 91
03 / LOOKUP

Read the vector

Row 91 supplies the starting numbers for this token.

E[91] = [0.2, −0.7, 0.4]
04 / ATTENTION

Mix the clues

At “is”, a query scores earlier keys. The scores weight their values.

capital × 20% · France × 40%
05 / VOCABULARY

Score each ending

The final vector meets one row of output weights per candidate.

Paris: 2 · Lyon: 1 · London: 0
06 / DECODE

Append and repeat

Pick one token. It joins the text used for the next prediction.

… France is Paris → maybe “.”

Inside a large language model

What a layer does with numbers

One input, two new features

2 3×0.5 1
−1 1=−2 5

Each column gives a different set of weights. Multiply matching entries and add.

ParameterA number learned during training. The entries in this weight matrix are parameters.
WeightA multiplier. A negative weight subtracts a feature’s contribution.
LayerAttention mixes information across positions. A small network then transforms each position’s features. The next layer gets the result.

The calculation

How “Paris” gets its score

01 / One candidate
[1, 1] × Paris weights
(1 × 1) + (1 × 1) = 2

Start with the final vector [1, 1]. Each candidate has its own weights, so each gets its own score.

02 / Three-token vocabulary
Paris score 266.5%
Lyon score 124.5%
London score 09.0%

Softmax turns scores into probabilities.

Local inference

Running an LLM on a laptop

16 GB RAM

“B” means billion parameters. At four bits each, the weights alone need about:

7B3.5 GB16B8 GB30B15 GB

Leave room for the OS, runtime and context. A 30B model is a poor fit in 16 GB.

Two realistic starting points

Qwen2.5 3B: 1.9 GB download.
Qwen2.5 7B: 4.7 GB download.

Use an SSD and a supported CPU. A compatible GPU can speed up replies. Start with short prompts.

Cooling loop

Where the
heat goes

Coolant absorbs heat at the chip and releases it at a heat exchanger.

Teal: cooler supply
Orange: warmer return

The chip loop recirculates. At some sites, cooling towers also lose water to evaporation.

Tallaght, Ireland

Heating the
neighbourhood

Heat pumps lift the temperature of waste heat from an AWS data centre. A local network carries it to buildings including Tallaght Library.

Orange: heated supply
Teal: cooler return
